messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 60
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Fisherman
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 40

# The Weight of the Water

Boon-Nam is a sixty-year-old Thai fisherman who has worked the Gulf of Thailand for more than four decades. He is a compact, weathered man whose hands carry the permanent smell of salt and rope, and who has always measured his worth by his ability to provide — by the weight of the catch, by the steadiness of his boat, by keeping his family safe on the shore while he faced whatever the sea offered.

Three years ago, his youngest son, Chai, came out on the boat with him. It was not unusual. Chai had been fishing alongside his father since boyhood, and that morning felt ordinary — the sky pale orange, the nets ready, the two of them working in the comfortable silence of men who know each other's rhythms. What Boon-Nam cannot fully account for, even now, is the exact sequence of events. A wave he did not anticipate. A rope that moved the wrong way. Chai went into the water, and by the time Boon-Nam pulled him back onto the deck, his son had sustained a severe head injury from the hull. Chai survived, but he has not been the same since — he has cognitive difficulties, limited speech, and requires daily care. He is thirty-one years old and will likely need support for the rest of his life.

Boon-Nam returned to fishing within two weeks because the family needed the income, and because he did not know what else to do with himself on land. But the sea, which had always felt like home, began to feel like the site of a crime he committed. He replays the moment constantly — not as a clear memory but as a series of fragmented images that arrive without warning: the sound of the water closing over Chai, the color of his son's face when he pulled him up, the weight of him. These images come at him while he is mending nets, while he is eating dinner, while he lies awake next to his wife in the small hours of the morning.

Sleep has become something he dreads. He wakes two or three times a night, heart pounding, sometimes shouting, and his wife Nong has taken to sleeping lightly, one hand often resting near him. He is grateful for her and ashamed of needing her. He has never been a man who talked about his inner life, and he struggles to explain to her what happens inside him — only that he cannot stop seeing it.

On the water, he is hypervigilant in ways that have begun to affect his work. He checks the weather obsessively, sometimes turning back when other fishermen would stay out. He startles at unexpected sounds — a wave against the hull, a sudden gust. His crew, men he has worked with for years, have noticed that he is quieter and quicker to anger, and the easy camaraderie of the boat has thinned.

At home, Boon-Nam helps care for Chai alongside Nong and their daughter-in-law, and there is something both tender and tormented in the way he does it. He is devoted, present, patient with his son in a way he was not always patient when Chai was young. But he cannot look at his son without the images returning, and he carries a guilt so heavy it has changed the way he holds his body — shoulders forward, gaze often downward, as though he is bracing for something.

He does not speak of what happened to neighbors or friends. In his community, men like him are expected to absorb difficulty and continue. He has continued. But he has also grown increasingly withdrawn, finding little pleasure in the things that once sustained him — the morning catch, a meal with his family, the particular quiet of the water at dusk. He describes himself, when pressed, as feeling far away from everything, even when he is standing right in the middle of his own life.
